candidate_item.vignette: A 13-year-old girl is evaluated after several episodes of carpopedal spasm. She has short stature, obesity, a round face, and shortened fourth metacarpals. Laboratory studies show low serum calcium, high serum phosphate, and markedly elevated parathyroid hormone despite normal renal function. Her mother has similar skeletal features and required calcium treatment during adolescence. Genetic testing identifies an inactivating variant in GNAS inherited from her mother.
candidate_item.lead_in: Which cellular signaling abnormality most directly explains this patient's biochemical findings?

options.A: Constitutive activation of the calcium-sensing receptor in parathyroid chief cells
options.B: Failure of parathyroid chief cells to synthesize parathyroid hormone
options.C: Reduced Gs-alpha stimulation of adenylate cyclase after parathyroid hormone receptor activation
options.D: Constitutive activation of the parathyroid hormone receptor in renal tubular cells
options.E: Reduced vitamin D receptor binding to DNA in intestinal epithelial cells

candidate_item.tested_construct: GNAS-mediated PTH resistance in pseudohypoparathyroidism type Ia

item.lead_in: Which intracellular signaling abnormality most directly explains these findings?

options.A: Reduced Gs-alpha stimulation of adenylyl cyclase after PTH receptor activation
options.B: Reduced synthesis and secretion of PTH by parathyroid chief cells
options.C: Constitutive Gs-alpha activation with persistent adenylyl cyclase signaling
options.D: Increased calcium-sensing receptor activity that suppresses PTH release
options.E: Defective CYP27B1-mediated conversion of vitamin D to calcitriol

item.tested_construct: Inactivating GNAS-related defects can reduce Gs-alpha signaling downstream of the PTH receptor. Impaired stimulation of adenylyl cyclase lowers the cAMP response to PTH, producing end-organ PTH resistance despite elevated circulating PTH.

item.vignette: A child has short stature, round facies, shortening of the fourth and fifth metacarpals, hypocalcemia, hyperphosphatemia, and an elevated parathyroid hormone concentration. A disorder of GNAS inactivation is suspected.

item.lead_in: Which molecular abnormality best explains this patient's findings?

options.A: Loss of function of the paternally inherited GNAS allele without hormone resistance
options.B: Loss of function of the maternally inherited GNAS allele with impaired Gs-alpha signaling
options.C: Activating mutation of GNAS causing constitutive Gs-alpha signaling
options.D: Loss-of-function mutation of the calcium-sensing receptor
options.E: Inactivating mutation of the PTH gene causing reduced hormone secretion

item.tested_construct: In tissues such as the renal proximal tubule, Gs-alpha is preferentially expressed from the maternal GNAS allele. Maternal GNAS loss of function impairs receptor-coupled adenylyl cyclase signaling, producing resistance to PTH and other Gs-coupled hormones together with Albright hereditary osteodystrophy.

candidate_item.vignette: A 4-year-old boy has recurrent fasting hypoglycemia, poor weight gain, and progressive diffuse hyperpigmentation. Serum cortisol is very low and plasma ACTH is markedly elevated. Serum sodium and potassium are normal. Genetic testing identifies a biallelic pathogenic variant in MC2R. His adrenal glands are structurally normal on imaging.
candidate_item.lead_in: Which molecular defect most directly explains this patient's low cortisol concentration?

options.A: Constitutive activation of the mineralocorticoid receptor in the distal nephron
options.B: Failure of the adrenal ACTH receptor to reach the cell surface or bind ACTH effectively
options.C: Loss of 21-hydroxylase activity with accumulation of 17-hydroxyprogesterone
options.D: Constitutive activation of the glucocorticoid receptor in peripheral tissues
options.E: Failure of the pituitary corticotroph to synthesize ACTH

item.difficulty_basis: Difficulty assigned during documented fresh item-by-item clinical audit.
item.lead_in: Which molecular defect most likely explains this patient’s disorder?

options.A: Loss of function of the melanocortin 2 receptor, preventing normal adrenal responsiveness to ACTH
options.B: Loss of 21-hydroxylase activity causing impaired cortisol and aldosterone synthesis with androgen excess
options.C: Autoimmune destruction of the adrenal cortex causing loss of both glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid production
options.D: Loss of the glucocorticoid receptor causing generalized cortisol resistance with elevated circulating cortisol
options.E: Loss of ACTH production by pituitary corticotrophs causing secondary adrenal insufficiency

item.tested_construct: Biallelic loss-of-function MC2R variants impair the adrenal ACTH receptor. The adrenal cortex therefore cannot respond normally to ACTH to generate glucocorticoids, causing very low cortisol with markedly elevated ACTH and hyperpigmentation. Mineralocorticoid secretion is classically preserved, distinguishing isolated ACTH resistance from global primary adrenal destruction or many steroidogenic defects.
item.vignette: A 3-year-old boy is evaluated after recurrent fasting hypoglycemia and poor weight gain. His skin and gingiva are diffusely hyperpigmented. Morning serum cortisol is very low and plasma ACTH is markedly elevated. Serum sodium and potassium are normal, plasma renin activity is normal, and aldosterone is appropriate for sodium intake. He has no ambiguous genitalia or history of salt-wasting crises. His parents are first cousins.

findings.explanation: Same asymptomatic familial hypercalcemia/hypocalciuria, CASR loss and shifted PTH/renal calcium sensing set point.

candidate_item.vignette: A 31-year-old woman is referred for persistent mild hypercalcemia discovered on routine testing. She feels well. Serum parathyroid hormone is in the upper-normal range despite the elevated calcium concentration. Twenty-four-hour urinary calcium excretion is low. Her father and two siblings have similar laboratory findings without nephrolithiasis. Genetic testing identifies a heterozygous loss-of-function variant in CASR.
candidate_item.lead_in: Which physiologic change most directly explains this patient's findings?

options.A: Increased sensitivity of parathyroid cells to extracellular calcium, causing excessive suppression of PTH
options.B: Increased renal calcium excretion due to exaggerated calcium-sensing receptor signaling
options.C: Autonomous PTH secretion from a monoclonal parathyroid adenoma
options.D: Reduced sensitivity of parathyroid and renal cells to extracellular calcium, shifting calcium feedback to a higher set point
options.E: Reduced intestinal calcium absorption due to impaired vitamin D receptor signaling

candidate_item.tested_construct: Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia due to loss of CaSR function

item.difficulty_basis: Difficulty assigned during the documented fresh item-by-item clinical audit.
item.lead_in: Which of the following physiologic changes best explains this patient's laboratory findings?

options.A: An increased calcium-sensing set point for suppression of parathyroid hormone together with increased renal calcium reabsorption
options.B: Autonomous parathyroid hormone secretion from a monoclonal parathyroid adenoma with increased urinary calcium
options.C: Constitutive activation of the calcium-sensing receptor causing excessive suppression of parathyroid hormone
options.D: Loss of parathyroid hormone receptor signaling in renal tubules causing hypocalcemia and hyperphosphatemia
options.E: Excess calcitonin secretion causing increased renal calcium excretion and reduced bone resorption

item.tested_construct: Heterozygous loss-of-function CASR variants raise the extracellular-calcium set point required to suppress parathyroid hormone secretion and increase renal tubular calcium reabsorption, producing mild lifelong hypercalcemia with inappropriately normal or mildly elevated PTH and relative hypocalciuria.
item.vignette: A 27-year-old woman is found incidentally to have mild hypercalcemia on repeated testing. She feels well. Parathyroid hormone is in the upper-normal range rather than suppressed, and urinary calcium excretion is low. Her mother and brother have the same biochemical pattern. Genetic testing identifies a heterozygous loss-of-function variant in CASR.
